title: The Three Questions That Make Any Passage Teachable
excerpt: You do not need a commentary or a seminary degree. You need three questions you can ask of any text, and the discipline to let the room answer them.
body:
Here is the lie that keeps ordinary believers from making disciples: that to open the Bible with others you first need to master it. You picture the requirement as a wall of commentaries, a working knowledge of Greek, a theological vocabulary you do not have. So you wait. And the waiting becomes a lifetime of silence.

The truth is that almost any passage of Scripture becomes teachable with three questions. Not clever questions. Not expert questions. Three plain questions that work on a parable, a psalm, a letter from Paul, a hard verse in the Old Testament. Learn them, and you can lead a study of anything.

## The method behind the questions

The three questions are a simple version of something pastors call inductive study. Inductive means you let the text speak first and draw conclusions from it, rather than arriving with conclusions and hunting for verses to prop them up. You observe before you interpret, and you interpret before you apply. The order matters, because skipping observation is how people make the Bible say whatever they already believed when they walked in.

Ezra "set his heart to study the Law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10). Study, do, teach, in that order. The three questions follow the same path.

## Question one: What does this show us about God?

Start here, always. Every passage in Scripture is, finally, revelation about God, his character, his actions, his heart, his holiness, his mercy. So you ask: what does this text show us about who God is and what he is like?

This question saves the table from the most common error, which is to read the Bible as though it were primarily about us, a self-help manual with God as a supporting character. It isn't. It is God's self-disclosure. When you read the parable of the prodigal son and ask what it shows about God, the answer is staggering: a father who runs. That answer reframes everything before you get anywhere near application.

Let people answer freely. There are usually several true answers, and the conversation that finds them is itself formative.

## Question two: What does this show us about people?

Now turn the mirror. What does the passage reveal about human beings, about our condition, our sin, our need, our possibility? And press it toward the room: what does it show about us, about me?

This is where self-implication enters, and it must. The forbidden move is to read the indictment as though it applies to other people, to the Pharisees, to the crowd, to whoever is not in the room. Scripture does not let us off that easily. When David's prophet Nathan told the story of the stolen lamb, David burned with anger at the man in the story until Nathan said, "You are the man" (2 Samuel 12:7). Every good Bible study eventually arrives at "you are the man," and the leader who has not let it land on himself first has no business asking it of anyone else.

Ask this question of yourself before the table meets. Then you ask it honestly, from inside the indictment, not above it.

## Question three: What does this ask of us this week?

The third question moves to obedience, but carefully. The danger here is the clean application turn, the neat little lesson, the tidy takeaway that makes everyone feel they have done something by merely naming it. Avoid the smooth version. Ask instead for something specific and costly. Not "we should love people more" but "who specifically do you need to forgive, and what will you do about it before Sunday?"

James warned about the man who looks in the mirror and walks away forgetting what he saw, and called the blessed one the doer who acts (James 1:22-25). The third question exists to make doers. Keep it concrete, keep it personal, and let people leave with something real to obey, not a sentiment to admire.

## How to actually run it

Read the passage aloud, twice if it's short. Then walk the three questions in order, slowly, and here is the hard discipline: do not answer your own questions. Ask, then wait. The silence will feel unbearable to you and not to anyone else. Count to ten in your head before you rescue the room. The answers that come after the long silence are almost always better than the one you were about to supply.

When someone says something off, you don't have to correct it like a referee. Just ask, "Where do you see that in the text?" The passage itself does the correcting, and the person learns to check their thinking against the page rather than against your authority.

## Why three is enough

You could ask thirty questions. You don't need to. These three cover the whole arc of how Scripture forms a person: it reveals God, exposes us, and calls us to obey. God, people, this week. A new believer can learn this in one evening and lead it the next. That is the point. The three questions are not just a way to study the Bible. They are a tool you hand to the people you disciple so that they can go disciple someone else without you in the room.

## This week

Pick one short passage, try the parable in Luke 15:11-32. Before your table meets, answer all three questions yourself, in writing, especially the second one about you. Then at the table, ask the three, in order, and after each one, count to ten before you speak.

You are not the expert in the room. You are the one who knows the three questions, and who has the nerve to stay quiet long enough for the Word to answer them.
